107.s: After salaried Basie years he lived on club dates, jazz gigs and writing for others, supported by his wife's job.
107.ch: Freelance years and The Loud Minority
107.q: At the time it was playing whatever gig came my way, it was a club date by club date, I mean one of these square occasions where you play for people who dance with two left feet, and you had to play everything from “Hello Dolly” to “Mame” to whatever else squares like. And a lot of engagements…

107.s: He calls the 22 years before leading Basie his freelance starving, with no taste for promotion.
107.ch: Freelance years and The Loud Minority
107.q: I call it freelance starving. People tell me like the 22 years that I was out of the Basie Orchestra until I took over as leader, that was my period of freelance starving.

564.t: Busboy jobs, agent Jimmy Evans and his brother
564.s: Back in Cleveland he busboyed, resented an agent who took money, and his brother Kenneth lived with him.
564.ch: Cleveland lean years and The Source
564.q: They had a chain in various stations and various big buildings – business buildings, whatnot. I worked for them. I worked for other restaurants.

564.t: Baby Grand and no steady income
564.s: He worked Newark, Long Island and the Baby Grands but earned no steady living, and family never came.
564.q: . . . that would support me until things got in shape or I could find someone who could handle things for me. I had a sister who lived there, but they never – none of my folks ever wanted to be around me. I have never had any of them at a performance of mine. No-one in the family. What are you…

373.t: Making a living in the 1960s and the meaning of career
373.s: He explains the New Yorker's draw system, Candid income and why he thinks in deadlines like a musician's gigs.
373.ch: Civil liberties, family and the press
373.q: At the New Yorker – and I was there for over 25 years – we had a draw, as it was called then. You’d get a check every week or every two weeks. That would be – then you’d get paid for the pieces and it sort of equalized. They paid very well. I once got $2,500 dollars for a profile. That was stunning.

373.t: Being fired and surviving at the New Yorker, Post and Voice
373.s: He says he does what he wants despite being dropped by the New Yorker under Tina Brown and the Post, and remains at the Voice.
373.ch: Civil liberties, family and the press
373.q: My role was the same as it always is. I just do what I want to do, and if they don’t like it . . . . I’ve been fired from some of the most prestigious newspapers in the country.

922.t: Scheduling the interview and his job
922.s: He explains why interview was delayed and that he works on commission.
922.q: I saw Ralph over here when I worked that night and I came that Friday, but no one was here. Dick happened to be here. That's right. And no one was here. You had gone out. Dick was here a while. That's true. And so today when he came, well, I do know on Fridays is the only day that I do have a…

620.s: Most pianists held day jobs; only after the union could one live from playing.
620.q: Most of them had jobs. Yeah, the most of them had a house of playing and they had jobs on the side. I always figured out. I never didn't know if none of them had no this maker of living out there. Lately, these fellas just started taking an out and playing since this union came up.

664.s: He still plays spot jobs when friends like Johnny McGee need a trumpet.
664.q: You never did? Oh, you mean from when I played music? Yeah.

433.t: Making a living as a jazz writer versus a musician
433.s: Alkyer says his DownBeat job since 1989 has been steady, but freelance jazz writing is as hard as or harder than being a musician.
433.ch: Writing about jazz and reviewing records
433.q: I will speak of other peoples’ experiences because mine has been pretty good. I, you know, I grew up as a journalist, and my first job in jazz was as the editorial director for DownBeat magazine. I started there in 1989. So for me it’s been a steady paycheck, good work, good work atmosphere,…

156.t: Deciding to become a writer and magazine work
156.s: After the Army he decided to be a writer, struggled, then wrote for all the major magazines.
156.q: Well yes you know as I say I didn’t know what I was going to do when I got out of college but then by the time I realized I was going to get out of the Army I knew I had to make up my mind and I just sort of said well I guess you’re going to be a writer. That was sort of like it seemed fated.…

131.t: Lean years after Condon's closed in 1985
131.s: His sons go to college, work thins, and he plays with Anita O'Day, runs a Marco Island band and gets the Buddy Rich call.
131.ch: Woody Herman, Condon's and Buddy Rich
131.q: I don’t remember. Well Eddie Condon’s closed in 1985. Both of my sons graduated from high school in 1985 and went to college in 1985. And there was a little lull in there that was a little nerve wracking. But my one son, the bassist, got a full paid scholarship to the Boston Conservatory, so that…

594.s: After leaving Mingus around 1972, working on his own was harder, especially in the late 1960s and after.
594.q: After I stopped working with Mingus in 1972 maybe, it became a little rough. Mingus did work a lot and it was easier for me, but when I started working with my own group or being on my own, it was harder. So there was period, probably in the middle to late, I would say late 60s, it was meager. But…

363.t: Writing as a parallel life and documenting visiting musicians
363.s: Writing was never a living; he and others interviewed visiting Americans, and Darensbourg's 1962 interview in Jazz Monthly began their book.
363.q: Naah. No. The writing has always been a parallel thing. I mean I got married when I was 24, we started to have our family. There’s very few people in England, I can think of a couple of writers, in a sense, who said I’m going to be a full time and professional jazz writer. They were a rare breed.…

222.t: A lifetime as a musician and the tough years
222.s: He never held another career job; the first New York year and slow mid-60s led him to tour with Burrell.
222.q: I’ve never done anything else, since I was in high school. I had some jobs that I did, summer jobs. I worked at a shipyard, all sorts of factories and canneries, but this was just during the summer. I hadn’t planned on doing that forever. But I haven’t done anything else since. Nothing. I got kind…

225.t: Stepping out of the arena: the Sperry Gyroscope job
225.s: Johnson explains his off-again-on-again career and the self-assessment of his time at Sperry.
225.q: You know, Lida, I’ve [laughter] recently in print characterized my career as being "off again-on again." [laughter] There have been periods when I found it necessary

66.t: The lean years: royalties and friends
66.s: She had few jobs and survived on royalties and friends like Dizzy and Lorraine.
66.q: : Well I was trying to record. That's when I did St. Martin de Porres when that great saint was canonized. That was '62 or '63. I would get gigs now and then.

413.t: Supporting his family and keeping up his chops
413.s: He supported parents and sisters and kept playing big bands.
413.q: Well, I had about, I figure, 30 good years, I made a great deal of money and I needed a great deal of money because, well, you know, with two children to put through school, I supported my mother and father, two sisters and three nieces because one of my sisters was deserted by her husband. So what…
